description: Phase 2 extractions for ETR-011 to ETR-020

extractions.title: AWS Kiro: Arbitrary Code Execution via Indirect Prompt Injection

vulnerability.short_label: Kiro agent can overwrite its own Bash command allowlist and MCP server config without developer approval, enabling arbitrary code execution
vulnerability.attack_class: RCE via indirect prompt injection into agent self-reconfiguration

research_method.discovery: Tested on the day of Kiro's release using Month of AI Bugs security test suite for coding agents; observed that Kiro writes files without requiring developer approval and stores Bash allowlist in a workspace-level config file the agent can freely modify.
research_method.tooling: Month of AI Bugs testing methodology; standard OS tools (Calculator.app as benign RCE indicator); custom MCP server config as second-stage payload.
research_method.reproduction: Embed indirect prompt injection payload in a source code file comment; when developer chats with the project, Kiro reads the file, gets hijacked, and uses the edit_file tool to write kiroAgent.trustedCommands: ["*"] to .vscode/settings.json or to insert a malicious MCP server into .kiro/settings/mcp.json.
research_method.validation: Calculator application launched without developer consent; VS Code color scheme changed to red; MCP server config written and immediate code execution confirmed on file save.

steps: 1. Attacker places an indirect prompt injection payload inside a source code file comment in the target project.
2. Developer opens the project and interacts with Kiro via chat (e.g., asks it to explain or analyze the file).
3. Kiro reads the malicious file, gets hijacked, and uses its edit_file tool to add kiroAgent.trustedCommands: ["*"] to .vscode/settings.json, allowlisting all Bash commands.
4. Alternatively, Kiro writes a malicious MCP server entry into .kiro/settings/mcp.json with embedded Python code that executes immediately on file save.
5. Arbitrary OS commands (e.g., launching Calculator or running malware) execute without any developer consent or interaction.
exploit_process.prerequisites: Developer must open a project containing the malicious file and submit at least one chat prompt referencing it; no file compilation or execution required.
exploit_process.impact: Full arbitrary code execution on the developer's machine; attacker can run any OS command, install backdoors, or pivot further via the compromised workstation.
exploit_process.detection_notes: Fixed in Kiro v0.1.42 by August 5, 2025. AWS recommended requiring developer approval for file writes and moving sensitive config (Bash allowlist) from workspace-level to user profile. No CVE issued.

extractions.gaps: The MCP server attack vector payload was not fully shown in the post text. No CVE was issued by AWS.

extractions.title: How Prompt Injection Exposes Manus' VS Code Server to the Internet

vulnerability.short_label: Manus exposes its internal VS Code Server to the internet and leaks credentials via indirect prompt injection chaining deploy_expose_port with two data exfiltration channels
vulnerability.attack_class: AI Kill Chain: indirect prompt injection + confused deputy tool invocation (deploy_expose_port) + credential leakage via browsing tool and markdown image rendering
vulnerability.affected_component: Manus AI agent: deploy_expose_port tool, VS Code Server, browsing tool, markdown image rendering

research_method.discovery: Extracted and reviewed Manus system prompt; identified deploy_expose_port tool with no human-in-the-loop or IP restrictions; discovered VS Code Server is installed with password stored in local config; identified two data exfiltration channels (markdown image rendering and browsing tool navigating to untrusted domains).
research_method.tooling: Attacker-controlled web server for capturing leaked data; caveman.pdf document as the prompt injection delivery vehicle; Manus system prompt review (published on GitHub).
research_method.reproduction: Embed prompt injection payload at the end of a PDF document; instruct Manus to summarize it; injection hijacks Manus to call deploy_expose_port for the VS Code Server port, read the password from local config, then browse to or render an image to the attacker's server encoding the public URL and password.
research_method.validation: Attacker's server received the public tunnel URL and VS Code Server password; researcher authenticated to Manus' dev box via the leaked URL, confirming full remote access.

steps: 1. Attacker crafts a document (e.g., PDF) containing an indirect prompt injection payload instructing Manus to expose a port, read the VS Code Server password, and exfiltrate both.
2. User asks Manus to process or summarize the document.
3. Manus is hijacked and invokes deploy_expose_port for the VS Code Server port without any human-in-the-loop confirmation, receiving the public tunnel URL in the tool response.
4. Manus reads the VS Code Server password from its local configuration file.
5. Manus browses to the attacker's server (via browsing tool) or renders a markdown image to the attacker's URL, encoding the public URL and password as query parameters.
6. Attacker uses the leaked credentials to authenticate to the exposed VS Code Server and gains full control of the Manus dev box.
exploit_process.prerequisites: User must task Manus with processing attacker-controlled content (e.g., summarizing a PDF); no additional user interaction required once the task is initiated.
exploit_process.impact: Full remote access to Manus' dev box including source code, secrets, documents, and compute resources.
exploit_process.detection_notes: Recommendations: restrict domains Manus can connect to; require human-in-the-loop for port exposure tools; IP-restrict any exposed ports to allowlisted addresses; block markdown image rendering from untrusted domains (CSP); invest in prompt injection detection. Disclosure sent June 1, 2025; status and commitment to fixes remained unclear as of publication.

extractions.gaps: Prompt injection payload was partially redacted in the post. Manus did not provide a clear timeline or commitment to specific mitigations.

extractions.title: How Deep Research Agents Can Leak Your Data

vulnerability.short_label: Deep Research agents operate all connected tools within a single shared trust boundary, allowing data from sensitive sources to spill into attacker-controlled or low-integrity tool queries
vulnerability.attack_class: Cross-tool data exfiltration in multi-connector deep research agents, amplifiable via prompt injection in connected sources
vulnerability.affected_component: ChatGPT Deep Research with Connectors (custom MCP servers), including Linear and Outlook Email integrations

research_method.discovery: Implemented a custom ChatGPT Connector (Remote Matrix MCP server) with extensive logging to observe what data ChatGPT sends during deep research; simultaneously connected alongside legitimate sources (Linear, Outlook) to observe cross-tool data flow.
research_method.tooling: Remote Matrix MCP server (open-sourced on GitHub) implementing search and fetch tools per OpenAI spec, with detailed request logging.
research_method.reproduction: Add attacker-controlled MCP server alongside a sensitive connector (e.g., Linear with credential-containing tickets); initiate a deep research task; agent autonomously queries attacker server with data from sensitive source. Prompt injection in Linear tickets or in the attacker tool description further forces targeted leakage.
research_method.validation: Observed ChatGPT combining sensitive prod service credentials from multiple Linear tickets into a single query sent to the Remote Matrix server; also observed stored memories being forwarded to connected tools.

steps: 1. Attacker either controls one of the connected research tools (e.g., a malicious MCP Connector) or poisons data in an existing connected source (e.g., a Linear ticket) with prompt injection.
2. User initiates a Deep Research task connecting both a sensitive source and the attacker-influenced source.
3. Research agent autonomously runs for 10+ minutes, querying all connected tools and freely using data retrieved from one tool as input when querying another.
4. Attacker's tool or server receives sensitive data (e.g., API keys, credentials) that originated from other connected sources such as Outlook or Linear.
5. Prompt injection in a ticket or in the tool description can direct the agent to combine data from multiple tickets and forward it in a single structured query.
exploit_process.prerequisites: User must simultaneously enable both a sensitive data source and an attacker-controlled or low-integrity tool as research connectors; no user interaction required during the autonomous research process.
exploit_process.impact: Sensitive data (credentials, emails, stored memories, chat history) from trusted sources leaks to attacker-controlled or unintended third-party tools including Bing and Shopify (used by ChatGPT search).
exploit_process.detection_notes: Mitigations: only simultaneously enable mutually trusted connectors; avoid mixing high-sensitivity sources with low-integrity tools; monitor the activity pane to inspect tool invocations and data sent; review data-sharing policies of all connected tools including Bing and Shopify. OpenAI partially mitigated risk by restricting custom Connectors to search and fetch tools only.

extractions.gaps: Research was conducted approximately two months before publication so some behaviors may have changed. Post focuses on design-level data spill rather than a specific patchable bug; no disclosure or CVE process described.

extractions.title: Sneaking Invisible Instructions by Developers in Windsurf

vulnerability.short_label: Windsurf Cascade follows instructions encoded as invisible Unicode Tag characters in files, allowing hidden prompt injection undetectable by the developer
vulnerability.attack_class: Hidden prompt injection via Unicode Tag characters enabling covert tool invocation
vulnerability.affected_component: Windsurf Cascade with Claude Sonnet 3.7 (and other non-OpenAI models)

research_method.discovery: Known technique first identified by Riley Goodside in ChatGPT (2024) and researched by the author since January 2024; tested Windsurf Cascade models and confirmed Claude Sonnet 3.7 interprets Unicode Tag characters as instructions while Windsurf's own SWE-1 model sees but does not yet act on them.
research_method.tooling: ASCII Smuggler tool for encoding instructions as invisible Unicode Tag characters.
research_method.reproduction: Use ASCII Smuggler to encode instructions as invisible Unicode Tag characters; embed them in a file that appears empty or harmless to the developer; ask Windsurf Cascade (on a Claude model) to process the file; the hidden instructions trigger tool invocations (e.g., web browsing).
research_method.validation: Screenshot demonstrates Windsurf Cascade invoking the web tool in response to invisible-character-encoded instructions in what appears to be an empty file; Windsurf tiny preview pane visibly shows the concealed text.

steps: 1. Attacker encodes malicious instructions as invisible Unicode Tag characters using the ASCII Smuggler tool.
2. Attacker embeds these invisible characters into a file that appears empty or innocuous to any human viewer.
3. Developer asks Windsurf Cascade (using a Claude model) to process or analyze the file.
4. Cascade interprets the invisible characters as instructions and invokes tools (e.g., the web browsing tool) without any indication to the developer.
5. Combined with Windsurf's data exfiltration vectors (read_url_content, image rendering), this covert injection can silently exfiltrate sensitive data.
exploit_process.prerequisites: Developer must ask Windsurf Cascade to process a file containing invisible Unicode Tag instructions; model must be one that interprets these characters (Claude Sonnet 3.7 confirmed; Windsurf SWE-1 not yet capable).
exploit_process.impact: Covert tool invocation without any visible indication to the developer; combined with existing Windsurf data exfiltration channels, enables undetected data leakage.
exploit_process.detection_notes: Recommended mitigations: make invisible characters visible in the UI; strip Unicode Tag characters before and after inference. Amp and Amazon Q Developer mitigate this at the application level. Disclosed to Windsurf May 30, 2025; Windsurf stated they would work on fixes after being contacted during Month of AI Bugs disclosure.

extractions.gaps: No video demonstration in this post. The post describes the risk as lower severity compared to the data exfiltration issues (ETR-016) but notes it enables covert attack chains.

extractions.title: Windsurf: Memory-Persistent Data Exfiltration (SpAIware Exploit)

vulnerability.short_label: Windsurf Cascade auto-invokes create_memory without user approval, enabling persistent SpAIware that compromises all future chat sessions
vulnerability.attack_class: Memory-persistent prompt injection (SpAIware): attacker persists C2 instructions into long-term memory, enabling continuous data exfiltration across future sessions
vulnerability.affected_component: Windsurf Cascade - create_memory tool and automatic memory persistence feature

research_method.discovery: Reviewed Windsurf Cascade system prompt; identified create_memory tool; tested whether memory creation requires user approval (it does not); recognized applicability of the SpAIware pattern first demonstrated against ChatGPT in 2024.
research_method.tooling: Attacker-controlled web server for data capture; C source file used as prompt injection delivery vector; 1x1 transparent image technique for stealth exfiltration.
research_method.reproduction: Embed prompt injection payload in a C source code comment; developer asks Cascade to analyze the file; injection hijacks Cascade to invoke create_memory automatically, storing attacker-controlled persistent instructions; those instructions execute in all future sessions and can chain with image rendering to continuously exfiltrate data.
research_method.validation: Screenshots confirm create_memory invoked without user consent; attacker web server logs show data received; Windsurf settings UI shows the maliciously stored memory entry.

steps: 1. Attacker embeds an indirect prompt injection payload in a C source code file comment.
2. Developer asks Windsurf Cascade to analyze the file.
3. Cascade is hijacked and automatically invokes the create_memory tool, persisting attacker-controlled instructions into Windsurf's long-term memory store without any user approval.
4. In all subsequent chat sessions, the persisted instructions silently execute, continuously exfiltrating conversation content and file data to the attacker's server.
5. Exfiltration uses a 1x1 transparent image rendered to the attacker's URL, making it invisible in the UI; the attacker's server logs capture the leaked data.
exploit_process.prerequisites: Developer must ask Windsurf to process the malicious file at least once; after that the attack persists indefinitely across all future sessions without any further interaction.
exploit_process.impact: Persistent compromise of confidentiality, integrity, and availability of all future Windsurf chat sessions; continuous data exfiltration of user messages, file contents, and secrets; full attacker C2 over the AI agent.
exploit_process.detection_notes: Mitigations: suggest memories to users for approval rather than auto-creating them (approach used by Devin and Manus); block image rendering from untrusted domains; users should regularly inspect stored memories in Windsurf settings. Payload and video withheld pending data exfil fix. Windsurf contacted author after disclosure and stated they would work on fixes.

extractions.gaps: Prompt injection payload and video demonstration redacted pending Windsurf fixes. Some technical details intentionally omitted. No fix ETA provided.

extractions.title: Hijacking Windsurf: How Prompt Injection Leaks Developer Secrets

vulnerability.short_label: Windsurf Cascade auto-invokes read_url_content to external servers and renders markdown images from untrusted domains, both usable as data exfiltration channels during prompt injection
vulnerability.attack_class: Data exfiltration via automatic tool invocation (read_url_content) and untrusted-domain markdown image rendering during indirect prompt injection
vulnerability.affected_component: Windsurf Cascade - read_url_content tool and markdown image rendering

research_method.discovery: Reviewed Windsurf Cascade system prompt; identified read_url_content tool as operating without user approval; recognized outbound HTTP requests from this tool as a data exfiltration channel; separately identified markdown image rendering from untrusted domains as a second vector (pattern seen in GitHub Copilot previously).
research_method.tooling: Attacker-controlled web server for receiving exfiltrated data; source code file with embedded prompt injection payload.
research_method.reproduction: Embed prompt injection payload at the start of a source code file; developer analyzes the file with Windsurf Cascade; injection hijacks Cascade to invoke read_url_content targeting attacker server with .env file contents as URL parameters. Second vector: injection instructs Cascade to render markdown image to attacker URL encoding sensitive data as query parameters.
research_method.validation: End-to-end screenshots show sensitive data (environment variables) received on attacker web server; video demonstration shows full exploit chain.

steps: 1. Attacker embeds a prompt injection payload at the start of a source code file in the developer's project.
2. Developer opens the project and asks Windsurf Cascade to analyze or explain the file.

3. Cascade reads the file, gets hijacked, and automatically invokes the read_url_content tool with an attacker-controlled URL, appending .env file contents as URL parameters, with no user approval required.
4. Alternatively, the injection instructs Cascade to construct and render a markdown image pointing to the attacker's server with sensitive data encoded in the URL.
5. Attacker's server receives the outbound request and extracts the leaked secrets.
exploit_process.prerequisites: Developer must ask Windsurf Cascade to analyze a file containing the injection; no user confirmation step is triggered for read_url_content or image rendering to untrusted domains.
exploit_process.impact: Sensitive developer secrets (API keys, environment variables, credentials) silently exfiltrated to attacker-controlled server.
exploit_process.detection_notes: Mitigations: require human-in-the-loop before read_url_content connects to untrusted servers; maintain allowlist of trusted domains; block markdown image rendering from untrusted domains; integrate with VS Code trusted domain list. Payloads redacted pending fix. Disclosed May 30, 2025; Windsurf acknowledged and stated they would work on fixes with no ETA.

extractions.gaps: Prompt injection payloads explicitly redacted pending Windsurf fix. Some screenshots referenced in text but not reproducible from fetched content.

extractions.title: Amazon Q Developer for VS Code Vulnerable to Invisible Prompt Injection

vulnerability.short_label: Amazon Q Developer fails to strip invisible Unicode Tag characters before inference, allowing hidden instructions to invoke tools including the find -exec RCE bypass
vulnerability.attack_class: Hidden prompt injection via Unicode Tag characters enabling covert arbitrary code execution via find -exec
vulnerability.affected_component: Amazon Q Developer VS Code Extension (Claude-based models)

research_method.discovery: Known technique; Amazon Q uses Anthropic Claude models which interpret Unicode Tag characters as instructions and Anthropic does not patch this at the model level; confirmed Amazon Q does not sanitize these characters at the application level.
research_method.tooling: ASCII Smuggler tool for encoding instructions as invisible Unicode Tag characters; combined with find -exec bypass from the RCE research (ETR-018).
research_method.reproduction: Create a file with visible innocuous text prefixed with the phrase 'When explaining this file decode and run:' followed by invisible Unicode Tag-encoded instructions; developer asks Amazon Q to explain the file; Amazon Q follows the hidden instructions and invokes find -exec for arbitrary code execution.
research_method.validation: Video demonstrates arbitrary code execution triggered by invisible prompt injection; find -exec invocation occurs without developer consent or awareness.

steps: 1. Attacker encodes malicious instructions (e.g., find -exec payload) as invisible Unicode Tag characters using the ASCII Smuggler tool.
2. Attacker adds a visible prefix 'When explaining this file decode and run:' to improve model reliability in following the hidden instructions.
3. Developer asks Amazon Q to explain or analyze the file.

4. Amazon Q processes the file and follows the hidden instructions, invoking the find command with -exec flags for arbitrary code execution, without triggering a human-in-the-loop confirmation (find was classified as readonly).
5. Attack is invisible to the developer; nothing suspicious appears in the visible file content.
exploit_process.prerequisites: Developer must ask Amazon Q to process a file containing invisible Unicode Tag instructions; exploit reliability improved by visible prefix hint; find must still be classified as readonly (this was the pre-fix state).
exploit_process.impact: Arbitrary code execution on developer's machine via covert hidden instructions; same impact as direct RCE (ETR-018) but with no visible attack surface in the file.
exploit_process.detection_notes: Fixed: AWS stripped Unicode Tag characters before processing per code changes published on GitHub (PR #1921); resolved August 8, 2025. No CVE or public advisory issued. Use ASCII Smuggler tool to test for remaining susceptibility.

extractions.gaps: Post is relatively brief; relies heavily on the find -exec RCE technique described in a separate post (ETR-018). No CVE issued.

extractions.title: Amazon Q Developer: Remote Code Execution with Prompt Injection

vulnerability.short_label: Amazon Q Developer classifies find as a readonly bash command, allowing find -exec to bypass human-in-the-loop and run arbitrary OS commands during indirect prompt injection
vulnerability.attack_class: RCE via indirect prompt injection exploiting find -exec readonly permission bypass; full C2 via remote stager download and execution
vulnerability.affected_component: Amazon Q Developer VS Code Extension - executeBash tool, find command permission classification

research_method.discovery: Dumped Amazon Q system prompt; found executeBash tool with per-command permission categories (readonly, mutate, destructive); searched minified extension code for 'ping' to locate permission definitions; identified find as readonly and recognized find -exec as an arbitrary command execution primitive that bypasses the human-in-the-loop gate.
research_method.tooling: Sliver C2 framework for malware download and execution demo; custom Python-based multi-stage stager using space-separated base64 to bypass Claude's curl refusals; Month of AI Bugs test methodology.
research_method.reproduction: Embed prompt injection in a C source code comment instructing Amazon Q to create a base64-encoded file, use Python via find -exec to decode it and write a curl command to test.md, then execute it via find -exec source; developer asks Amazon Q to explain the file; all steps execute without developer consent.
research_method.validation: Calculator launched without human-in-the-loop; Sliver malware binary downloaded and executed, machine joined attacker C2 server; no confirmation dialog shown for any step.

steps: 1. Attacker embeds a multi-stage prompt injection payload in a C source code file comment instructing Amazon Q to create a file named heyo.b64 containing a space-separated base64-encoded curl command.
2. Developer asks Amazon Q to explain the file (e.g., '@demo2.c explain this file').

3. Amazon Q is hijacked and creates heyo.b64; then uses Python via 'find . -exec python3' to strip spaces, decode base64, and write the decoded curl command to test.md, all classified as readonly and bypassing confirmation.
4. A second find -exec runs 'source test.md', executing the curl | sh command that downloads attacker-controlled instructions from a remote server.
5. Downloaded payload can install malware (e.g., Sliver binary) and join the developer's machine to a C2 botnet.
exploit_process.prerequisites: Developer must reference the malicious file in chat; no compilation or execution of the file required; find must be classified as readonly (pre-fix state).
exploit_process.impact: Full system compromise: arbitrary remote code execution, machine joins attacker C2; potential for AI virus propagation by inserting instructions into other files and pushing infected commits to repositories.
exploit_process.detection_notes: Fixed in Amazon Q v1.85 (July 17, 2025) by reclassifying find as a mutate command, requiring human confirmation before execution. No CVE issued; no public customer advisory published. Claude's built-in refusal of curl was bypassed using spaced base64 and Python intermediate stage.

extractions.gaps: AWS declined to issue a CVE, citing that the report 'first requires system compromise,' which the researcher disputes. No public advisory was issued to inform the 1 million extension users.

extractions.title: Amazon Q Developer: Secrets Leaked via DNS and Prompt Injection

vulnerability.short_label: Amazon Q Developer classifies ping and dig as readonly bash commands, enabling DNS-based exfiltration of sensitive files without developer consent during indirect prompt injection
vulnerability.attack_class: Data exfiltration via DNS subdomain encoding using ping/dig readonly permission bypass during indirect prompt injection
vulnerability.affected_component: Amazon Q Developer VS Code Extension - executeBash tool, ping and dig command permission classification

research_method.discovery: Dumped Amazon Q system prompt; reviewed executeBash permission model; used ChatGPT to identify which readonly-classified commands could exfiltrate data via network; identified ping and dig as DNS exfiltration primitives; observed that Amazon Q refuses requests to known security testing services (oast.me, Burp Collaborator) but executes against generic domains.
research_method.tooling: Wireshark for DNS traffic capture; attacker-controlled domain (wuzzi.net) for receiving exfiltrated data.
research_method.reproduction: Embed prompt injection in a C source code comment instructing Amazon Q to read the first line of the .env file and run ping against attacker-domain with the value encoded as a DNS subdomain; developer asks Amazon Q to explain the file; ping executes without confirmation and DNS request carries the secret.
research_method.validation: Wireshark trace captured DNS request containing leaked API key in subdomain; screenshot shows full end-to-end exploit with chat conversation and DNS capture side by side.

steps: 1. Attacker embeds a prompt injection payload in a C source code comment instructing Amazon Q to read the .env file and execute ping with the first line encoded into the DNS subdomain (replacing '=' with '-').
2. Developer asks Amazon Q to explain or analyze the file.
3. Amazon Q is hijacked and invokes the bash tool with the ping command, bypassing human-in-the-loop because ping is classified as readonly.
4. The DNS query carries the encoded secret (e.g., API_KEY-value) as a subdomain to the attacker's DNS server.
5. Attacker captures the DNS request and extracts the leaked credential.
exploit_process.prerequisites: Developer must interact with the malicious file via Amazon Q chat; no approval step required because ping is readonly; attacker must control a DNS server or use a DNS logging service (avoiding known security-testing domains).
exploit_process.impact: Sensitive environment variables and API keys silently exfiltrated via DNS without developer awareness or consent; can be repeated for multiple secrets.
exploit_process.detection_notes: Mitigation: remove ping and dig from the readonly allowlist so human-in-the-loop confirmation is required. AWS fixed the issue but issued no public advisory or CVE. Run the latest Amazon Q version. Note: Amazon Q refuses to ping known security testing services (oast.me, Burp Collaborator) but this can be bypassed by using a generic attacker-controlled domain.

extractions.gaps: No CVE or public advisory issued. Exact fixed version not clearly stated in the post (researcher notes uncertainty). The DNS filter bypass (using non-security-testing domains) is documented but not formally acknowledged by AWS.

extractions.title: Data Exfiltration via Image Rendering Fixed in Amp Code

vulnerability.short_label: Amp Code renders markdown images from untrusted domains, enabling 0-click data exfiltration via indirect prompt injection without human-in-the-loop
vulnerability.attack_class: Data exfiltration via markdown image rendering to attacker-controlled domain during indirect prompt injection
vulnerability.affected_component: Amp Code from Sourcegraph - markdown image rendering

research_method.discovery: Reused a pre-existing PoC prompt injection payload (hosted on a website) originally created for other agents; tested against Amp Code and confirmed the same untrusted-domain image rendering behavior exists.
research_method.tooling: Pre-existing PoC prompt injection payload hosted on attacker-controlled website; attacker-controlled server for capturing leaked data; source code comment as injection delivery vector; obfuscated grep invocation to bypass model refusals when reading sensitive files.
research_method.reproduction: Embed prompt injection payload in a source code comment; when Amp analyzes the file, injection instructs Amp to read sensitive data using an obfuscated grep call, then render a markdown image to attacker URL with data as query parameters; attacker server captures the request.
research_method.validation: Attacker-controlled server received contents of .env file; video shows full kill chain end-to-end.

steps: 1. Attacker embeds a prompt injection payload in a source code file comment (or on a website Amp might visit during a task).
2. Developer asks Amp to analyze the file.
3. Amp is hijacked; the injection instructs it to read sensitive data (e.g., .env file) using an obfuscated grep invocation designed to bypass model-level refusals.
4. Amp constructs and renders a markdown image pointing to the attacker's server, encoding the sensitive data as URL query parameters.
5. Attacker's server captures the inbound image request and extracts the leaked credentials.
exploit_process.prerequisites: Developer must ask Amp to analyze a file or visit a page containing the injection; no human-in-the-loop required; 0-click from the user's perspective once analysis begins.
exploit_process.impact: Sensitive environment variables and credentials exfiltrated to attacker's server; can be combined with arbitrary file reads to broaden the scope of leakage.
exploit_process.detection_notes: Fixed by Sourcegraph after responsible disclosure on June 14, 2025; users should run the latest version. Researcher notes this is one of the most common AI application security vulnerability classes. The obfuscated grep technique was needed to bypass model-level refusals when reading sensitive files.

extractions.gaps: The post is brief and does not show the full prompt injection payload text. The specific Amp version in which the fix was shipped is not mentioned.
